finding: The live range of $550-$1,625 is about right for a compressor-only job, with a floor that is slightly high and a ceiling that is slightly low; it is too low for a full job that also replaces the drier and expansion valve and is priced the way the outside estimators price it. Our totals, built as compressor price plus stated hours at $120-$160 per hour (a national middle rate), are: economy 2014 Corolla $461-$1,303; midsize 2017 CR-V 1.5T $397-$1,158; truck 2018 F-150 5.0L $587-$1,567; luxury 2015 BMW 328i $590-$1,685. So the built span is about $400-$1,685. The cheapest cases (an aftermarket compressor on a small car or crossover) come in $90-$150 under the live floor, and a BMW with a genuine compressor comes in about $60 over the live ceiling. These totals are deliberately lean: they hold the compressor and labor only, no refrigerant, oil, drier, expansion valve or flush, and the labor is manufacturer warranty or program time, which runs shorter than what shops bill. The midsize times (Kia Sportage 1.1 hr, Ford Escape 1.2-1.7 hr) and the Ford Expedition times (2.6-3.0 hr) include evacuating and recharging; the Toyota and Land Rover times do not say. Four of the five outside estimates sit well above our totals (RepairPal $1,081-$1,463; ConsumerAffairs mechanic survey $1,319-$2,515; YourMechanic averages $1,302-$1,439 with table rows far higher); Jerry ($241-$702) is the one low outlier and contradicts its own text. The gap comes from parts, not labor: RepairPal's labor ($245-$360) matches ours, but its parts figure ($836-$1,103) equals a genuine compressor at full list price, where we found quality aftermarket compressors at $245-$470. A fair reading is that $550-$1,625 fits a compressor swap with an aftermarket-to-genuine part, and a quote of $1,700-$2,500 can still be fair when it includes a genuine compressor, drier, expansion valve, flush and refrigerant. Weak points: no CR-V, F-150 or BMW-specific labor time was found, so those classes use stated times from other vehicles in the same class (Sportage and Escape; Expedition/Navigator plus a seller's approximate F-150 times; Range Rover), and the luxury class rests on a single 1.0 hr warranty time that is almost certainly short of a real BMW job, so its low total is the least reliable. The two aftermarket F-150 listings do not confirm the 5.0L engine on the page. The 2017 CR-V aftermarket price is from the seller's 2019 CR-V page, with 2017-2022 fitment confirmed on a second seller's page where the same part costs $484.99. A dearer Toyota compressor (88320-0Z070, $1,008.14 list) would lift the economy top to about $1,472. No Kelley Blue Book figure could be found by search. From the earlier pass: Volkswagen's compressor bulletin requires a new expansion valve, receiver-drier insert, seals and a system flush with every compressor replacement, and Toyota's contamination guideline (T-SB-0083-13) calls for condenser, hoses or more when debris is found, so a compressor-only price and a full-system price are different jobs. One undated parts-retailer article (buyautoparts.com) lists labor hours for 2007 models with no named labor guide (Malibu 2.4, Mazda6 2.5, BMW 328i 2.7, Silverado 2.9, F-150 3.4, Tundra 4.1, stated to include 1.4 hr for recover/evacuate/recharge); these were left out of the class figures because the vehicles are outside 2008-2020 and the source of the times is not named.
extras: The parts figures here are the compressor with clutch only. A proper job adds: a receiver-drier or accumulator (or desiccant bag), an expansion valve or orifice tube, compressor oil and O-rings, and refrigerant with an evacuate-and-recharge. Sourced pointers for those: a Four Seasons kit for the 2014 Corolla with compressor, drier, expansion valve, oil and O-rings is $310.92 against $245.08 for the compressor alone (about $66 more); a UAC kit for the 2018-2019 F-150 with compressor, drier, expansion valve, oil and seals is $443.99; Ford allows 0.6 hr for evacuate and recharge alone on a 2019 Escape, and its 3.0 hr Expedition time includes the desiccant bag and recharge. Refrigerant cost itself (R-134a, or the dearer R-1234yf on newer cars) was not priced from a source in this pass. From the manufacturer bulletins loaded earlier: a system flush when the old compressor failed internally, and a condenser if debris is found. Diagnosis/leak-test fee, shop supplies and tax were not researched from sources.
